item.title: NIST Releases Final IR 8547 Establishing Definitive Post-Quantum Cryptography Transition Timeline and Deprecation Schedules
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because NIST’s final IR 8547 turns the long‑running PQC standardization effort into a concrete policy timetable that will force every federal system—and eventually most commercial services—to replace RSA/ECDSA with quantum‑resistant algorithms within the next decade. The deadlines align with recent breakthroughs in lattice‑based and code‑based schemes that have cleared security evaluations, making the transition technically feasible while still giving vendors time to implement hybrid deployments. By flagging “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” threats, the roadmap underscores an urgent risk for any organization still relying on classical public‑key crypto, prompting immediate migration planning. Readers should note that while the schedule is binding for U.S. agencies, global adoption will likely follow, reshaping key‑management ecosystems worldwide.

NIST has released its final roadmap, NIST IR 8547, for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards, with federal agencies facing binding deadlines to adopt PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and digital signatures by December 31, 2031. Classical public-key algorithms will be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035. The report emphasizes the urgency of PQC adoption due to "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" attacks and provides guidelines for hybrid schemes during the transition. By pairing Quantinuum’s Helios hardware with GE Vernova’s materials expertise, the collaboration could accelerate the discovery of new high‑temperature superconductors that would improve efficiency in wind turbines, marine propulsion and grid components—areas where classical methods struggle with electron correlation complexity. While still early‑stage and limited by qubit count and error rates, the work demonstrates how quantum computers are beginning to tackle materials challenges that have long been bottlenecks for clean‑energy technologies.

Quantinuum and GE Vernova are collaborating to model high-temperature superconductivity (HTS) using Quantinuum's Helios quantum computer. This partnership aims to overcome limitations of classical simulations by directly executing Fermi–Hubbard simulations, leveraging Quantinuum's quantum hardware and GE Vernova's materials expertise. The research seeks to identify novel HTS materials with industrial applications in wind generators, marine propulsion, and grid infrastructure. item.title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reveals that the many‑body states generated during routine dynamical simulations carry a hidden layer of quantum information that can be harvested for tasks such as encoding bits, tracking entanglement growth, and even estimating communication rates. By showing how simple spin‑chain protocols already act as miniature quantum memories—especially contrasting the exact fermionic covariance reconstruction in XX models with richer spin‑measurement readouts in XXX chains—the work bridges the gap between traditional response‑function calculations and emerging quantum‑information diagnostics. The insight opens a practical pathway for experimental platforms to extract additional value from existing simulation runs, though realizing full communication‑rate estimates will still require careful control of measurement back‑action and noise.

Dynamical quantum simulations are commonly designed to access a particular response function or correlation function. Yet the underlying protocol prepares a family of many-body states that contains information well beyond the observable for which the simulation was originally designed. In this work, we explore the idea of using these states as laboratories for quantum information. As a case study, we consider the local-pulse protocols used to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, and we interpret opposite source rotations as encoding a classical bit into the many-body system. This allows us to follow how the resulting record propagates, how it is encoded across local subsystems, and how readily it can be accessed with different measurements. We also find a clear separation between representation and readout. While fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed response in the XX chain, simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of the locally available information in the XXX chain. This reversed ordering persists when we move from finite-pulse discrimination to local source-angle estimation. Going beyond the source record, the same reduced states also allow us to reinterpret results in terms of Bell state recovery and quantum communication rates, as well as providing direct access to the evolving bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement of the system. Our results show that dynamical quantum simulations developed for response calculations can naturally be used to ask a much broader set of quantum-information questions about the many-body states they already prepare.

item.title: Security Analysis of Ekert-type QKD Protocol Coming Under Cloning Attacks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article sharpens our understanding of how entanglement‑based QKD—specifically Ekert’s protocol—holds up when an eavesdropper employs sophisticated asymmetric cloning attacks on one or both photons, a scenario that mirrors realistic side‑channel threats in emerging quantum networks. By mapping out which two‑qubit states still yield a positive Devetak–Winter key rate under such attacks, the work bridges theoretical security proofs with practical hardware constraints and informs the design of more robust entanglement sources for future deployments. The findings also echo recent efforts in device‑independent QKD to certify secrecy despite imperfect devices, though they remind readers that not all entangled states are equally resilient, so careful state engineering remains essential.

We analyze the security of an Ekert type bipartite key distribution protocol coming under cloning attacks by an untrusted observer. Precisely, an eavesdropper is assumed to intercept and apply an asymmetric, phase-variant cloner on one or both qubits which are transmitted over public channel from an authenticated source to the trusted parties. We partially characterize two-qubit states from the perspective of designing a QKD protocol that can generate a distillable secret key among the trusted users even under such cloning attacks. We rely upon Devetak Winter framework for computing key rate so as to identify states, which when used in the protocol, secret-key can be distilled. Utility of an entangled state, for designing a successful QKD protocol, changes from single-qubit to double-qubits cloning attacks. Interestingly, we can distinguish some useful families of two-qubit entangled states when only one of the transmitted qubits is cloned by a malicious third party.

item.title: Prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution from a bound on information leakage
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a single quantitative bound on how much information leaks from the sender’s lab—rather than a detailed physical model of the source—is enough to prove security against collective attacks in prepare‑and‑measure QKD. By removing assumptions about state dimension, energy or purity and only requiring that Bob’s measurement does not leak data, the authors bridge the gap between fully device‑independent schemes and practical implementations, extending recent semi‑device‑independent work on side‑channel mitigation. The resulting protocols achieve secret‑key rates comparable to BB84 (tolerating up to 8 % QBER) while simplifying hardware requirements, though they do require new designs because the standard B92 and BB84 cannot be certified under this minimal leakage assumption.

Every quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol must limit the information available outside the users' laboratories. In device-independent QKD this is essentially the only assumption made on the devices. In a prepare-and-measure setting it cannot be imposed strictly, since the sender's device must emit a signal that depends on her private input. The natural replacement, and a minimal one, is a leakage bound: a bound on how much information about the input leaves the sender's laboratory, through the intended signal or through any side channel. We ask how far this unavoidable requirement can replace a detailed model of the source. We show that this single bound, quantified by the probability of guessing the input from everything the source emits, suffices to prove security against collective attacks. In our analysis, nothing is assumed about the precise form of the emitted states, their dimension, energy or purity, nor about the receiver's measurement device, beyond the standard requirement that it does not leak Bob's data. The standard B92 and BB84 protocols do not certify any key under this minimal leakage bound assumption. But closely related protocols can and, in the ideal limit, achieve one secret bit per key round. For noisy implementations, we compute key rates using semidefinite programming relaxations. Our best protocols tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, corresponding to an 8% quantum bit error rate, compared with the 11% threshold of standard device-dependent BB84.

item.title: Experimental evidence for quantum Brownian motion in electron-metal decoherence
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first experimental confirmation that quantum Brownian motion drives decoherence of free electrons near metal surfaces, finally realizing a proposal that has lingered for two decades. By showing tunable electron‑metal decoherence and matching Caldeira‑Leggett predictions, it establishes microchannel electron beams as practical open‑quantum systems for free‑electron quantum optics—a platform that could sharpen the resolution limits of next‑generation electron microscopes and inform error models for electron‑based qubits. The work also provides a new testbed for dissipation theories, though scaling the approach to more complex architectures will be needed before it can directly impact large‑scale quantum computing hardware.

Feynman once remarked that the double-slit experiment has in its heart the only mystery of quantum mechanics. Arguably, the scientific significance of double-slit experiments lies in motional decoherence and the mechanism behind it. Decoherence of motional states underpins our understanding of quantum-to-classical transition. It is also central to the operation of miniaturized quantum electron devices and poses a resolution limit for electron microscopes. In this work, we provide experimental evidence for the critical role of quantum Brownian motion in electron motional decoherence. We demonstrate, for the first time, clear signatures of electron-metal decoherence and its continuous tunability. Our experiment concludes a two-decade long search for experimental realization of the Anglin-Paz-Zurek proposal, establishing electron-microchannel systems as viable open quantum platforms for free-electron quantum optics. The quantitative agreement between experiment and theory further paves the way for testing the Caldeira-Leggett quantum dissipation theory with free electrons.

item.title: Deployed entanglement-based BBM92 quantum key distribution using frequency-converted photons emitted by a quantum dot
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first field‑tested BBM92 QKD system that combines a GHz‑rate, polarization‑entangled photon pair source from an epitaxial quantum dot with quantum frequency conversion to telecom wavelengths, delivering a stable 206 Hz secure key over a 1.59 km deployed fiber link. By achieving more than 14 Mbit of error‑corrected key in 19 hours, the work demonstrates that solid‑state emitters can rival traditional spontaneous‑parametric‑down‑conversion sources while offering on‑chip scalability for future hybrid quantum networks. The result is a concrete step toward practical, information‑theoretic security in existing fiber infrastructure, though further improvements in conversion efficiency and long‑distance loss will be needed to compete with metropolitan‑scale QKD deployments.

Establishing secure communication is an important requirement in existing and future networks. Although current solutions rely on classical approaches, quantum mechanics offers the possibility of moving from computational to information-theoretic security. Quantum key distribution (QKD) has been extensively studied as a means of achieving such security. Recently, epitaxial quantum dots started to be studied and employed in quantum cryptography, because of their rapid development that made them one of the brightest sources of quantum light to date. In particular, they are known to be excellent sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, especially droplet-etched dots operating at $\sim$780 nm. Here, we employ such a quantum dot to generate entangled photon pairs under 1 GHz excitation rate. Using quantum frequency conversion, we interface the emitted photons with the telecommunication wavelength range while preserving their polarization entanglement. This enables quantum key distribution over a 1.59 km field-deployed fibre link across the University of Stuttgart - campus Vaihingen, using the BBM92 protocol: we achieve a secure key rate of 206 Hz over 19 h of stable operation, resulting in a total secure key length of 14.2 Mbit. This key enables the safe encryption and decryption of a colour image with further implementation of error correction and privacy amplification. These results demonstrate important steps towards hybrid quantum networks by combining high-quality entangled-photon sources operated at high excitation rates, efficient frequency conversion module, and picosecond-level time synchronization in a realistic deployed network.

item.title: HTM: A Hybrid Classical-Quantum Computation Model
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it offers the first formal framework—HTM—that unifies classical and quantum control logic into a single state‑transition model, something that has been missing despite growing interest in quantum‑accelerated workflows. By introducing standardized representations for hybrid states and a complexity metric based on entanglement and superposition, HTM directly addresses current pain points such as ad‑hoc task partitioning and hardware‑agnostic scheduling, complementing recent efforts like Qiskit Runtime and Azure Quantum’s orchestration services. If adopted, the model could streamline compiler design and system architecture across platforms, although its practical impact will hinge on how quickly near‑term quantum processors can support the required control‑sharing mechanisms.

Classical and quantum computers have achieved collaborative computation and completed applications across numerous fields. Nevertheless, the absence of a unified hybrid computation model has led to issues such as non-standardized engineering architecture design, ambiguous task partitioning criteria and so on. To address these issues, this research proposes a hybrid classical-quantum computation model (HTM). By constructing unified state sets and transition function representations, HTM clarifies hybrid control logic and implements a control-sharing mechanism. Simultaneously, a comprehensive complexity calculation method based on entanglement and superposition was proposed, supporting computation task partitioning and resource scheduling. The HTM fills a theoretical gap in the classical-quantum hybrid computation area and implements the joint promotion and development of computing models and hardware.

item.title: QNETSIM for memory assisted design of satellite and hybrid quantum networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first dedicated discrete‑event simulator that can jointly model orbital mechanics, free‑space optics, fiber links and realistic quantum memories—capabilities that have been missing from existing network tools as satellite‑based quantum experiments move from proof‑of‑concept to deployment. By exposing how memory capacity, decoherence rates and routing policies affect entanglement fidelity, throughput and latency, QNETSIM lets designers explore the trade‑offs needed for global quantum‑internet architectures, complementing recent milestones such as China’s Micius satellite and emerging low‑Earth‑orbit constellations. The framework’s modularity will accelerate prototyping of hybrid space‑ground protocols, though its predictions will ultimately hinge on accurate physical models and forthcoming hardware performance data.

Space-based quantum information networks require simulation tools that capture orbital dynamics, probabilistic quantum operations, and classical coordination. We introduce QNETSIM, a modular discrete-event simulator for the design and performance evaluation of satellite and hybrid space-ground quantum networks. The framework integrates orbital geometry, free-space optical and fiber channels, quantum memories, entanglement generation, and Bell-state measurements within a common event-driven architecture. Physical models account for optical loss, atmospheric turbulence, detector imperfections, finite memory capacity, and storage-induced decoherence. Space-time routing and segmented nesting support entanglement distribution across changing topologies, while a software-defined control plane coordinates generation, storage, and swapping. Configurable scenarios encompass onboard repeaters, satellite constellations, ground-based repeaters, and direct satellite distribution. Through explicit interfaces between physical models, network protocols, and orchestration, QNETSIM links component characteristics and operational policies to entanglement fidelity, throughput, latency, availability, and memory utilization, enabling systematic exploration of architectural and resource-management trade-offs in future space-based quantum information networks.

item.title: Generative quantum extreme learning machines
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that quantum generative models can sidestep barren‑plateau problems by adopting a quantum extreme learning machine approach in which only a linear readout layer is trained, leaving the bulk of the circuit fixed and random. By analytically comparing Clifford reservoirs, T‑gate‑doped circuits, and Haar‑random brickwork layers, the authors show that neither entanglement nor non‑stabilizer resources automatically improve generation quality, highlighting the central importance of the latent‑encoding strategy rather than raw circuit depth. The result offers a concrete, near‑term pathway for leveraging existing noisy quantum hardware in generative tasks while reminding researchers that clever encoding and architecture design remain essential for any practical advantage.

Training the circuit of a quantum generative model is hampered by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with the number of qubits. In the present work we propose a generative protocol based on the paradigm of quantum extreme learning machines, in which the circuit is never trained. A random latent vector is encoded into a quantum state, evolved with a fixed unitary and measured, and only a linear output layer is trained. The encoding of the latent variable determines the functions available to the model, while the unitary decides which combinations of them are seen by the trained layer. With the help of Pauli propagation we show that for a Clifford unitary each feature is a single product of sines and cosines of the encoded angles, so that a Clifford circuit, even a strongly entangling one, does not create new functions. Doping the circuit with $T$ gates mixes these products and changes the nonstabilizerness of the state, but the space of functions remains the one fixed by the encoding. For brickworks of Haar-random two-qubit gates the features are no longer single products, and their variation with the latent variable decreases with the depth of the circuit. For the proposed encoding and for one- and two-dimensional distributions, generated both from expectation values and from single measurements, neither the entanglement produced by a Clifford reservoir nor the additional nonstabilizerness of Haar-random brickworks systematically improves the generator, and a reservoir with no gates at all is competitive with entangling circuits.

item.title: Qubit-environment entanglement in pure dephasing dynamics for mixed initial states
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article expands the toolkit for diagnosing qubit‑environment correlations by showing how entanglement can arise even when a qubit starts in a mixed state and undergoes pure dephasing—situations that closely match real‑world superconducting or spin‑based hardware. By demonstrating that traditional separability criteria become merely witnesses in the mixed‑state regime, the authors reveal phenomena such as sudden entanglement birth that were previously thought impossible, and they provide a computationally cheap witness that scales to large baths. The results give experimentalists a more realistic way to quantify decoherence pathways and could help guide error‑mitigation strategies for near‑term quantum processors.

Decoherence of qubits is one main limitation in quantum information processing, where the qubits themselves can be mixed because of decoherence and additional decoherence may generated through interactions with a bath. Here, we present a complete study of qubit-environment entanglement in the case of interactions that lead to pure dephasing of the qubit by allowing the initial state of the qubit to be mixed, exceeding previous restrictions. We find that the criteria for separability that hold for pure initial states of the qubit are reduced to witness status. Yet, the evolution of the witnesses reflects the array of features that entanglement can exhibit in the mixed case but are forbidden in the pure-qubit case. Most notably, this includes sudden birth of entanglement as the initial phase of the evolution is typically separable. Moreover, there is a stark numerical advantage to the study of entanglement for large environments when using the witness rather than the traditional measures available. We include the study of entanglement generated between a spin qubit and a sparse spin environment to illustrate the peculiarities of the evolution of entanglement in this case, as well as to emphasize the level of reliability of the entanglement witness.

item.title: A Unified Protocol for Arbitrary Z Rotations of a Class of Bosonic cQED Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it offers the first systematic recipe that works for arbitrary Z‑rotations on a whole family of bosonic Fock‑based qubits rather than requiring bespoke pulse sequences for each encoding. By distilling the common structure into a six‑step protocol, the work streamlines calibration and could accelerate the integration of error‑corrected bosonic logical gates alongside recent advances in cat‑code and binomial‑code hardware. The result is a practical design rule—if an encoding satisfies the identified condition, developers can reuse the same control stack, lowering engineering overhead while still preserving the high coherence that makes bosonic qubits attractive.

Bosonic-qubit encodings provide diverse approaches to storing and processing quantum information, with logical operations often implemented through encoding-specific physical strategies. Here, we identify a class of bosonic Fock-based qubits in circuit QED for which distinct implementations of arbitrary Z rotations share a common structure. We formulate this structure as a six-step protocol that provides a unified procedure for implementing arbitrary Z rotations across this class of bosonic cQED qubits. The applicability of the protocol is determined by a specific condition on the encoding, providing a criterion for identifying bosonic Fock-based cQED qubits that admit the common implementation.

item.title: Effective Noise Thresholds for Reliable Quantum Approximation Optimisation Algorithm under Noisy Environment
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a quantitative “effective noise threshold” that marks the boundary between reliable and unreliable performance of QAOA as circuit depth increases, filling a gap left by prior studies that only asked how deep to go on a given device. By fitting noisy GPU‑accelerated simulations to a generalized logistic surface, the authors show that deeper QAOA layers demand dramatically lower error rates—a result that dovetails with recent findings on noise‑induced barren plateaus and helps practitioners pick an optimal depth before hitting diminishing returns. The framework also offers a practical diagnostic for real hardware such as IBM’s Marrakesh chip, pointing out which error channels dominate and guiding both algorithmic tuning and hardware improvement efforts.

Variational quantum algorithms are leading candidates for practical utilisation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors, but accumulating noise bounds the usefulness of circuit depths. For the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm (QAOA), this trade-off has mostly been addressed by searching for the best depth for a given device. In this work, we consider the inverse question: how much noise each depth can tolerate. Using GPU-accelerated noisy QAOA simulations for MaxCut on three graph families with 6 to 18 vertices, depths up to 10 and three noise channels, we fit the approximation ratios with a generalised logistic surface. We propose the effective noise threshold as the inflection boundary of the logistic surfaces, a noise boundary separating reliable and unreliable QAOA approximation regimes. In general, the threshold decreases as depth rises, indicating that deeper circuits demand for stricter noise requirement for reliable approximation. Its best and worst values over depth divide the noise axis into three regions: every depth remains effective, depth must be chosen with care, or no depth induces effective optimisation. Assessing on the ibm_marrakesh processor, although modelled gate errors understate factual noise, the threshold modeling remains beneficial in informing qualitative depth-dependence structure and identifying dominating noise channel in noisy QAOA.

item.title: Quantum Art Unveils Geometric Quantum Algorithm for Wave Propagation, Bypassing Condition-Number Bottlenecks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights a genuinely new approach: a geometric quantum algorithm that sidesteps the notorious condition‑number barrier in wave‑propagation simulations, allowing a quantum computer to prepare states directly on the resonant dispersion manifold. By promising exponential reductions in grid size—from 10^18–10^21 classical points down to roughly 100 logical qubits— it builds on recent advances in trapped‑ion error‑corrected architectures and could reshape high‑frequency acoustics, radar and seismic modeling if the hardware scaling materializes. The result is a concrete illustration of how algorithmic innovation can unlock practical advantages before raw qubit counts reach millions, though realizing the projected logical depth will still demand robust fault tolerance and near‑term improvements in ion‑trap connectivity.

Quantum Art has developed a geometric quantum algorithm for wave propagation that bypasses condition-number bottlenecks, outperforming classical supercomputers. This method, detailed in a research preprint, directly prepares quantum states on the wave equation's resonant dispersion manifold, making it suitable for applications like acoustics and radar. Their trapped-ion hardware architecture is projected to efficiently execute these complex circuits using approximately 100 logical qubits for problems requiring 10^18 to 10^21 classical grid points. item.title: Consensus And Information Redistribution In Quantum Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how decentralized quantum consensus can turn a sprawling qudit network into a self‑organising sensor that reveals global properties from purely local measurements, sidestepping the costly full‑state tomography that has limited many distributed‑quantum applications. By proving analytic conditions under which random unitary dynamics preserve specific global observables—and by demonstrating concrete CNOT and two‑qubit interaction schemes that recover excitation‑number moments—the work bridges a gap between abstract consensus theory and practical quantum hardware implementations. The results lay groundwork for scalable quantum internet protocols, distributed metrology, and fault‑tolerant state verification, although the reliance on idealized random unitaries means experimental validation will be an essential next step.

Consensus algorithms are mechanisms driving nodes of a network to agreement. In quantum networks they also redistribute information encoded in the global quantum state, allowing global properties to be inferred from local measurements without reconstructing the global state. Motivated by this, we investigate decentralized quantum consensus in qudit networks governed by discrete random unitary dynamics. We characterize the analytic asymptotic dynamics, identify global information preserved by the evolution, and derive conditions for which different notions of quantum consensus emerge. A general theorem is derived that establishes a unified framework for extracting globally encoded information from local measurements beyond consensus states. First, we analyze CNOT networks and determine which global information can be recovered by individual nodes and which requires joint measurements on cooperating nodes. The CNOT model is well understood and presents a case with entanglement creation - a characteristic quantum feature of networks worth analyzing in detail. Second, we identify the complete class of two-qubit interactions that asymptotically achieve consensus on the average number of excitations, thereby establishing a quantum analogue of classical average consensus. We further show that joint measurements on k cooperating nodes recover exactly the first k moments of the excitation-number distribution.

item.title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory for Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers a finite‑temperature quantum quasinormal‑mode framework that finally lets researchers rigorously quantize lossy, non‑reciprocal magnonic resonators while accounting for thermal fluctuations and open‑cavity radiation losses. By unifying the description of microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits, it bridges a key gap that has limited the design of hybrid quantum processors based on cavity magnonics. The theory predicts observable effects such as modal interference, a smooth transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, and even magnon‑mediated qubit synchronization—tools that can directly inform upcoming experiments in quantum transduction and networking. Its practical impact will depend on accurate material loss characterization and temperature control, but it offers a much-needed roadmap for scaling magnonic hardware into functional quantum technologies.

Cavity quantum magnonics has ushered in an unprecedented era of hybrid light-matter interfaces in which microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits can be coupled within a single device architecture, facilitating a versatile platform for quantum information processing. Realizing their full potential, however, requires a theory that can treat non-reciprocal magnetic media, material dissipation and open-cavity radiation losses, as well as finite-temperature fluctuations rigorously and without significant approximation. The dissipative magnonic resonances of such systems are described as quasinormal modes (QNMs), yet a consistent quantization procedure for lossy gyrotropic resonators has remained elusive. In this work, we present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory, based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media and complex coordinate transformations, that achieves QNM quantization for a wide class of spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative and dispersive, cavity magnonic systems. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our theory via applications to hybrid dielectric-magnonic resonators interacting with both spin and superconducting qubits, evidencing modal interference effects, a continuous transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization, at both zero and finite temperatures. By addressing the intricacies of modal loss and non-reciprocity in a fully quantum theory of cavity magnonics, our approach enables the quantitative design of hybrid quantum devices that operate under realistic open-system and thermal conditions, without recourse to ad hoc quantization schemes.

item.title: Suppressing microwave crosstalk in superconducting quantum processors by designing parasitic drive capacitances
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the “unwanted” parasitic capacitances in a superconducting chip can be turned into a tool for cancelling microwave drive crosstalk, offering a systematic circuit‑level strategy rather than ad‑hoc layout tweaks. By mapping all coupling pathways—including those through a tunable coupler—and demonstrating interference‑based suppression experimentally, the work provides concrete design rules that will help keep coherent error rates low as processors grow beyond a few dozen qubits. The approach promises to simplify hardware scaling and could reduce the need for costly calibration overheads in large‑scale quantum computers.

As superconducting quantum processors scale to large qubit counts, unwanted microwave drive crosstalk becomes an important source of coherent errors. Here, we investigate the role of parasitic coupling paths in the suppression of drive crosstalk in a processor with two fixed-frequency transmon qubits and a tunable coupler. To account for the many different coupling paths, we develop a detailed circuit model to capture the dependence of crosstalk on the coupler frequency. We experimentally demonstrate suppression of crosstalk, finding that the suppression does not originate solely from cancellation of the effective qubit-qubit coupling, but also is a result of interference between other coupling paths. Building on these insights, we show that drive crosstalk can be suppressed with the right choice of parasitic capacitances, which otherwise often are treated as unwanted design imperfections. Our results provide practical guidance for low-crosstalk device design of superconducting quantum processors and point toward a broader strategy in which parasitic coupling paths are engineered rather than simply minimized.

item.title: Modeling the CNOT gate in Germanium double quantum dots
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first detailed, fast‑time simulation of a CNOT gate built from exchange‑coupled hole spins in Ge/GeSi double quantum dots, showing how a compact dressed singlet–triplet basis can replace costly configuration‑interaction calculations. By pinpointing non‑adiabatic barrier ramps, AC Stark shifts and charge‑noise hotspots as the dominant fidelity killers, it gives concrete design targets for microwave driving and gate‑voltage control that are directly relevant to the emerging CMOS‑compatible spin‑qubit roadmap. The work therefore bridges theory and experiment, helping the community gauge how close germanium‑based platforms are to achieving the high‑fidelity two‑qubit operations needed for scalable quantum processors.

We model a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate mediated by exchange interactions in a realistic Ge/GeSi hole spin-qubit device. We use for that purpose a computationally efficient framework based on a compact dressed basis of many-body singlet and triplet states, which enables fast time-dependent simulations that would be prohibitive within a conventional configuration-interaction approach. We discuss the dominant sources of infidelity in ideal (noise-free) devices. On the one hand, the nonadiabaticity of the tunnel barrier ramps, enhanced by the transverse component of the exchange interaction, imposes limits on the speed of the CNOT gate. On the other hand, the AC Stark shift of the conditional resonance and the off-resonant driving of the complementary transition can significantly degrade the gate fidelity and call for a careful optimization of the driving conditions. Finally, we investigate the impact of quasi-static charge noise on the fidelity of the CNOT gate. We find that the capture of charges near the qubits can strongly disrupt the conditional operation, while the nanometer-scale motion of charges results in a loss of fidelity that sensitively depends on the position and strength of the corresponding dipole. Our results quantify the requirements on barrier control, microwave driving, and charge-noise stability for high-fidelity two-qubit operations in Ge/GeSi hole-spin qubits.

item.title: Twist-controlled imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a rigorously controllable way to trigger the imaginary‑time Mpemba effect in spin lattices by applying spatially patterned “twist” rotations that selectively populate high‑energy modes while leaving entanglement structure untouched. By isolating spectral‑weight redistribution as the sole driver of accelerated relaxation, the work provides a concrete analytical toolkit for speeding up ground‑state preparation—a long‑standing bottleneck for variational quantum imaginary‑time evolution and related algorithms. The authors validate the mechanism on interacting XXZ chains and even on a twelve‑qubit circuit simulation, suggesting that near‑term devices could exploit these twists to reduce convergence times without additional hardware overhead. While promising, practical deployment will still need careful calibration of twist profiles and error mitigation to preserve the delicate mode selection in noisy quantum processors.

We construct a controllable imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems using spatially modulated local rotations without changing initial bipartite entanglement spectra and correlation magnitudes. This feature unambiguously isolates the redistribution of spectral weights as the sole driver of the anomalous relaxation. Using the compact-boson description, we reveal that these twists act as precise mode selectors: higher-harmonic twists exclusively populate high-energy standing waves, structurally bypassing slow-decaying infrared modes to accelerate convergence. We derive exact analytical crossing times for these reversals and demonstrate that intentionally reintroducing the slow-mode population systematically delays the ITME. This exact mechanism is validated beyond the fixed-point theory via calculations on interacting XXZ chains and ladders. Furthermore, a twelve-qubit simulation of variational quantum imaginary-time evolution reproduces the reversals and their controlled delay, providing a concrete route to realize this protocol in realistic quantum circuits. Ultimately, these results provide a strictly controllable and exact starting point for realizing and investigating the imaginary-time Mpemba effect, establishing a foundational paradigm to harness anomalous non-equilibrium relaxation in quantum ground-state preparations.

item.title: Bell-pair distillation under imperfect operations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the Bell‑pair distillation protocol introduced last year can still boost entanglement fidelity even when the underlying gates and measurements are noisy, a crucial step toward deploying entanglement purification on near‑term hardware. By mapping out which incoherent versus coherent error regimes preserve the advantage—and revealing how asymmetric errors can be balanced through complementary postselection—the work links theoretical guarantees to realistic quantum‑network nodes and sensing platforms. The findings suggest that modest‑quality devices could already benefit from built‑in entanglement cleaning, though the protocol’s tolerance varies sharply with error type, underscoring the need for tailored calibration in practical deployments.

We recently proposed an entanglement distillation protocol based on local operations and classical communication that probabilistically and universally distills a maximally entangled Bell pair from multiple copies of an unknown two-qubit state [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 260202 (2025)]. Here, we investigate the robustness of this protocol against imperfections in its implementation. We consider several incoherent and coherent gate-error models, as well as measurement readout errors, and determine the regimes in which distillation enhances the fidelity with the target Bell state. We find that the protocol remains effective over substantial error ranges, although its robustness depends strongly on the type of error. We further analyze asymmetric errors between the two parties and identify conditions under which complementary postselection outcomes yield identical distillation dynamics, allowing the success probability to be enhanced.

item.title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route for extracting full energy‑level degeneracies and thermodynamic observables from noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices by measuring the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures with just a single ancilla qubit. By leveraging an exact inverse discrete Fourier transform on spectra that lie on an equally spaced grid, the authors avoid spectral leakage and achieve near‑exact reconstruction of degeneracies—even on a 36‑spin frustrated Kagome Ising model run on IBM’s Kingston processor—showcasing how clever circuit ordering can tame depth‑related noise. The result is a proof‑of‑principle that thermodynamic quantities such as heat capacity can be reliably estimated on current hardware, opening the door to quantum‑assisted studies of complex many‑body materials without requiring full phase‑estimation or large ancillary registers.

We propose a hybrid quantum-classical method for reconstructing energy-level degeneracies and thermodynamic properties of spin systems. A single ancilla qubit is used to measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures. For spectra lying on a known equally spaced energy grid, the inverse discrete Fourier transform allows exact reconstruction of degeneracies in the absence of noise, without spectral leakage. The quantum circuits are optimized using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering. We demonstrate the method for frustrated Ising antiferromagnets on periodic Kagome graphs with up to 36 spins, using the ibm_kingston quantum processor. Despite substantial circuit depth and hardware noise, the reconstructed spectra retain their dominant features, and the calculated heat capacities reproduce the main temperature dependence of the exact results. Keywords: partition function, imaginary temperature, Ising model, heat capacity, ancilla qubit, quantum computing.

item.title: Electron-photon entanglement in real space from quantum electrodynamics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first fully real‑space, time‑resolved simulation of electron–photon entanglement generated by scattering in a nonrelativistic QED framework, going beyond the usual rotating‑wave approximation and single‑mode models. By showing how the transient global entanglement peaks during an off‑resonant pulse while local entropy patterns map the dipole coupling strength, it provides a concrete benchmark for emerging waveguide‑QED platforms that aim to harness strong light–matter interactions for hybrid quantum processors. The results also clarify where photons are created and absorbed in space, offering practical guidance for designing nanophotonic structures that minimize decoherence while maximizing controllable entanglement.

We study the entanglement between an electron and the photon it scatters, resolved in real space and time. Starting from nonrelativistic QED in Fermi's oscillator representation, we write Fock's coupled equations for components with fixed photon number in the photon configuration space, in the length gauge, where the photon is created around the atom through a nonlocal kernel. Truncated at one photon, the equations are solved numerically without the rotating-wave approximation for a one-dimensional model atom in a waveguide with a single transverse mode and enhanced coupling. The atom is driven by a short, off-resonant laser pulse, with the electron and photon represented on real-space grids. The global electron-photon entanglement is largely transient. It peaks during the pulse and decreases as the polarized electron cloud returns to the core, leaving a state close to a product of the electron state and a superposition of the field vacuum with a single scattered photon. Local entanglement, obtained from walkers sampled across both photon-number components, exhibits opposite spatial patterns for the two particles. The electron entropy is smallest at the nucleus and maps the local strength of the dipole coupling, whereas the photon entropy is largest near the atom, where photons are created and absorbed, and smaller in the outgoing wave packets.

item.title: Multimode continuous-variable quantum key distribution with CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic integration
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first CMOS‑compatible multimode continuous‑variable QKD system, showing that silicon‑photonic transmitters and receivers can jointly generate and detect two polarization channels with >20 dB shot‑noise clearance and a finite‑size secret‑key rate of 6.7 Mbit/s over deployed fiber. By integrating a dual‑channel transimpedance amplifier and using digital unitary recovery to eliminate active polarization control, the work bridges the gap between laboratory‑scale QKD demonstrations and mass‑manufacturable hardware, echoing recent pushes toward fully integrated quantum communication chips. The multimode security analysis also reveals that modest crosstalk (≈2 %) can nearly double the secure distance compared with single‑mode estimates, highlighting a practical pathway to high‑throughput, scalable quantum‑secured networks. Readers should note that while the results are compelling, extending beyond two modes and maintaining low crosstalk will be key challenges for future deployments.

Multiplexing and photonic-electronic integration offer a route to scalable and high-throughput quantum key distribution (QKD) networks through parallel transmission and compact hardware suited to volume manufacturing. Realizing this route requires multichannel transmitters and receivers, and a security analysis accounting for mode coupling. Here we present a CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic multimode continuous-variable QKD architecture, using polarization multiplexing as a two-mode example. Silicon-photonic transmitter and receiver chips prepare and detect two polarization modes in parallel. The receiver is co-integrated with a dual-channel 28-nm CMOS transimpedance amplifier, providing shot-noise clearances exceeding 20 dB in both channels. Pilot-assisted unitary digital recovery removes the need for active optical polarization control, while a multimode security analysis accounts for the mode crosstalk. At 2 percent residual crosstalk, the multimode analysis extends the simulated secure distance from 39 to 84 km, near the crosstalk-free limit of 89 km. Over 10 km of deployed fibre, the mean total finite-size secret-key rate estimate is 6.69 Mbit/s, 12 percent above the single-mode analysis from the same digitally recovered data. These results establish a route to scalable multimode quantum-secured networks built on technology suited to mass production.

item.title: Quantum-Classical Framework for the Joint Optimization of Bidirectional EV Charging and Trip Assignment
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a hybrid quantum‑classical Benders decomposition can tackle the notoriously hard joint scheduling of bidirectional EV charging and trip assignment, introducing logic‑based conflict cuts that sidestep the qubit overhead normally required for feasibility constraints. By sparsifying the state‑of‑charge formulation and demonstrating MILP‑optimal results on benchmark problems—and even running a tiny instance on IBM’s quantum processor—the work bridges recent advances in quantum optimization (e.g., QAOA and annealing) with real‑world energy‑mobility challenges. While still at proof‑of‑concept scale, the approach hints that future quantum accelerators could become practical tools for managing distributed energy assets in smart‑grid fleets.

The integration of bidirectional (V2G) charging allows electric vehicle (EV) fleets to operate as distributed energy assets. However, the joint optimization of charging schedules and trip assignments is NP-hard. Moreover, bidirectional power flows create non-monotonic state-of-charge (SoC) dynamics that weaken standard dual-based Benders cuts. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical Benders decomposition framework. To overcome the qubit overhead associated with encoding feasibility cuts, we introduce logic-based conflict cuts, which require near-zero auxiliary qubits. Furthermore, we develop a sparse recursive SoC formulation that reduces the constraint-matrix density by a factor of T/3 in the horizon length T. We demonstrate that our framework recovers MILP-optimal solutions on benchmark instances with a low auxiliary-qubit budget, and, as a minimal proof of concept, we execute a small instance end-to-end on IBM quantum hardware.

item.title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a critical bottleneck for large‑scale superconducting processors by showing that both two‑qubit and single‑qubit gates can be driven with frequency‑division multiplexed microwave pulses, cutting the number of control lines needed by up to two orders of magnitude. The demonstrated 1:4 parallel CZ and XY(π/2) gate fidelities—6.4 × 10⁻³ and 1.06 × 10⁻³ respectively—match conventional single‑line performance, indicating that multiplexing does not sacrifice error rates. By completing an all‑microwave control stack, the work paves the way for denser qubit layouts within the limited cooling power of dilution refrigerators, a prerequisite for the millions of physical qubits required by fault‑tolerant architectures. The results still rely on careful band‑pass filtering and may need further scaling studies, but they provide a concrete path toward hardware‑efficient quantum error correction.

Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Comparing classical and quantum QUBO solvers: optimality, trajectory diagnostics, and limits of solver selection
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it provides the most systematic head‑to‑head benchmark yet between classical exact solvers, tensor‑network methods and a fixed‑schedule quantum algorithm on realistic QUBO instances up to 128 variables, revealing that mature branch‑and‑cut techniques still outpace current quantum approaches for solution quality and optimality certification. By dissecting trajectory diagnostics such as bond dimension growth and identifying warm‑start trapping in DMRG sweeps, the authors show where tensor‑network methods have untapped potential but also why simple rules for solver selection remain elusive. The finding that a linear‑ramp QAOA offers no advantage over classical comparators underscores the need for more sophisticated quantum schedules or hybrid strategies before quantum hardware can claim practical superiority on combinatorial optimization problems.

Comparing solvers for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) requires distinguishing solution quality from optimality certification. We compare classical, tensor-network, and fixed-schedule quantum approaches on 180 benchmark instances from ten families with 14-48 variables, supplemented by harder synthetic instances with known optimal solutions, extending to 128 variables. On the main benchmark, a general-purpose branch-and-cut solver matches all reference energies and certifies 176 instances within a 600,s cap. When the known optima are moved to randomly chosen bitstrings, the search comparison changes: at n = 48 the branch-and-cut solver finds only four of ten optima and certifies none, whereas parallel tempering reaches every optimum in every tested run at a 60,s budget. Structural and trajectory diagnostics explain aspects of tensor-network performance. A treewidth bound ranks trajectory bond-dimension demand at Spearman $ρ= 0.78$ in sample and $0.73$ out of sample, but provides only a coarse runtime estimate. Controlled experiments identify excited-state trapping during warm-started density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) sweeps and demonstrate mitigation by restarting the variational search. These diagnostics do not yield a validated solver-selection rule. The tested linear-ramp quantum approximate optimization algorithm (LR-QAOA) runs offer no solution-quality improvement over the classical comparators. In the separate Wishart scaling study, on the harder setting, none of the classical methods tested reaches the optimum at the sampled sizes from n = 72 onward within the tested budgets. While this does not provide evidence for quantum advantage, it identifies a domain for further investigation.

item.title: Modulation and protection of entanglement in a two-qubit system via two interacting oscillator control
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how deliberately coupling auxiliary harmonic oscillators can actively shape the decoherence landscape of two qubits, offering a rare analytical treatment that links oscillator stability to entanglement dynamics. By demonstrating regimes where position‑position and momentum‑momentum interactions revive or suppress concurrence—even in the presence of thermal dissipation—the work extends recent reservoir‑engineering approaches that use bosonic modes as protective “quantum buses.” If experimentally realized, such engineered oscillator networks could become a lightweight hardware layer for preserving entanglement on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum processors.

We investigate the control and protection of two-qubit entanglement through engineered interactions between two auxiliary harmonic oscillators. Each qubit is coupled to a local oscillator via a dephasing interaction, while the oscillators interact through independently tunable position-position and momentum-momentum couplings. Employing the characteristic-function representation, we obtain analytical solutions for the composite-system dynamics and examine how the stability properties of the coupled oscillators determine the evolution of two-qubit concurrence. Our analysis reveals distinct dynamical regimes exhibiting entanglement revivals, suppression, or decay, and identifies configurations in which oscillator interactions effectively reduce entanglement degradation. We further investigate the influence of thermal dissipation using local and global master-equation descriptions, demonstrating that suitable oscillator couplings can preserve substantial two-qubit entanglement under the dissipative conditions considered. These results establish a connection between the dynamical stability of auxiliary bosonic modes and the controllability of entanglement in discrete-variable quantum systems, providing a potential strategy for entanglement protection through engineered oscillator interactions.

item.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports a new technique that uses a supercurrent to perform a quantum‑non‑demolition readout of a qubit, allowing the state to be inferred without causing collapse. By leveraging dissipation‑free superconducting currents, the method sidesteps the trade‑off between measurement fidelity and back‑action that has limited many superconducting processors, complementing recent progress in dispersive readout and error‑corrected logical qubits. If scalable, such nondestructive sensing could simplify syndrome extraction in surface‑code architectures and reduce overhead for quantum error correction, though integration with existing control hardware remains an open challenge.

One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.
